reviewer.notes: Independent first-pass adjudication using only the blind packet. The six-card format was assessed explicitly against the continuous-summary construct.

passageAssessment.notes: The six cards give a coherent overview, but they are independent sentence completions, not a continuous summary. Their answers run strictly through all four paragraphs in passage order, which makes this a broad scanning bank rather than the usual bounded summary-completion section. Several removable modifiers also weaken exact one-best-answer control.

questions.completedSentence: Rooftop farming is increasingly visible in cities where there is unused roof space.
questions.competitorFailure: It omits the location modifier 'roof'; however, 'unused space' remains grammatical and is a literal subspan that preserves the broad claim, so there is no decisive exclusion.
questions.reasoning: The full noun phrase reproduces the passage precisely, but the head noun alone also completes the frame naturally and is passage-supported. The item therefore lacks a clean exact one-best answer.

questions.completedSentence: These farms may shorten food supply chains and help residents notice seasonal produce.
questions.competitorFailure: In the frame, 'chains' creates 'food chains', normally an ecological term, and drops the passage's distribution meaning.
questions.reasoning: The full two-word span is the only completion that retains the passage's precise logistical claim, although the nested one-word span may attract a superficial response.

questions.completedSentence: Careful irrigation and lightweight soil systems can reduce pressure on older buildings.
evidenceQuotes: reduce the strain on older buildings
questions.competitorFailure: It loses the age restriction, but the broader statement remains grammatical and logically follows from the passage.
questions.reasoning: The selected phrase is more precise, yet the literal head noun alone still yields a true completed sentence. Exact scoring would need to accept both or revise the frame.

questions.completedSentence: Rainwater collection can reduce demand for treated water.
evidenceQuotes: rainwater collection may lower the demand for treated water
questions.competitorFailure: It removes the qualifier 'treated', but the resulting statement is grammatical and entailed at a more general level.
questions.reasoning: The two-word answer matches the source claim exactly, while its one-word head is also a valid literal completion. This prevents exact one-best adjudication.

questions.completedSentence: Some projects have an educational role because schools use them for science lessons.
evidenceQuotes: Schools use them for science lessons
questions.competitorFailure: It omits the subject area, but 'schools use them for lessons' remains grammatical and passage-supported.
questions.reasoning: The fuller phrase is maximally faithful, but the nested head noun supplies a second defensible exact span under the same word limit.

questions.completedSentence: Before planting, successful projects often require engineers to check the roof.
questions.competitorFailure: The passage assigns care of the site to managers; it explicitly assigns checking the roof to engineers.
questions.reasoning: The agent-action relation and the temporal cue point uniquely to the final-paragraph clause.

passageAssessment.notes: The cards cover a sensible progression from purpose to preparation, benefits and operating principles, but they do not constitute one continuous summary. Answers appear in strict order and are distributed across the whole passage. Nested head nouns create multiple exact-span rivals in several items.

questions.completedSentence: Repair cafes help residents fix broken household objects with support from volunteers.
evidenceQuotes: residents brought broken household objects and learned how to fix them
questions.competitorFailure: It removes the household qualifier, but the broader completion is grammatical and still supported by the passage.
questions.reasoning: The full phrase is the closest reproduction, while the nested head noun remains independently acceptable in the frame.

questions.completedSentence: Visitors are usually asked to stay during the repair so the activity becomes a lesson instead of only a service.
evidenceQuotes: the event becomes a lesson rather than a free service
questions.competitorFailure: Staying during the repair is the condition; the passage says the event becomes a lesson, not that the activity becomes a repair.
questions.reasoning: The contrast with a service directly paraphrases the passage's lesson-versus-service opposition.

questions.completedSentence: Before a session, volunteers check whether common spare parts are available.
evidenceQuotes: check whether common spare parts are available
questions.competitorFailure: It omits 'spare', but 'common parts' remains grammatical and is a literal subspan of the same proposition.
questions.reasoning: The intended phrase is transparent, yet the stem already supplies 'common', allowing the head noun alone to convey a valid broader meaning.

questions.completedSentence: Electrical items should be inspected by people with relevant training.
evidenceQuotes: Electrical devices, for example, may be inspected only by people with relevant training
questions.competitorFailure: The phrase belongs to older residents' social contribution; the electrical-safety restriction explicitly requires training.
questions.reasoning: The equipment type, inspection action and adjective 'relevant' align uniquely with the safety sentence.

questions.completedSentence: Students may develop confidence when they use unfamiliar tools.
evidenceQuotes: students gain confidence with unfamiliar tools
questions.competitorFailure: Although grammatically plausible, that benefit is attached to older residents sharing knowledge, whereas the student clause names confidence.
questions.reasoning: A nearby benefit phrase can distract, but the parallel subjects in the source sentence establish the intended answer clearly.

questions.completedSentence: Many cafes protect the educational mood by focusing on shared problem solving.
evidenceQuotes: keep the focus on shared problem solving
questions.competitorFailure: Shared practical knowledge is a social benefit earlier in the passage, but the final operating principle explicitly names problem solving.
questions.reasoning: The educational-atmosphere cue links directly to the final paragraph, making the selected span clearly superior despite a plausible thematic distractor.

passageAssessment.notes: The six cards form a topical outline but not a continuous summary: each is an autonomous sentence. Answers follow the passage exactly from opening to closing paragraphs and therefore reward serial scanning. The intervention card admits more than one listed span, while several other cards permit shortened head-noun answers.

questions.completedSentence: Cities are mapping shade as heatwaves become increasingly frequent.
questions.competitorFailure: It is a singular mass phrase and therefore disagrees with 'become'; it also denotes a condition, not events becoming more frequent.
questions.reasoning: Number agreement and the opening causal clause identify the plural event noun uniquely.

questions.completedSentence: The process starts with satellite images, but teams also collect information on streets.
evidenceQuotes: The work begins with satellite images
questions.competitorFailure: It omits the source qualifier, but the resulting sentence is grammatical and supported at a broader level.
questions.reasoning: The full phrase is precise, while its literal head noun is also a defensible answer under the stated extraction rule.

questions.completedSentence: A short route may feel longer if pedestrians are exposed to direct sun for several blocks.
evidenceQuotes: it exposes pedestrians to direct sun for several blocks
questions.competitorFailure: It omits 'direct', but exposure to sun remains grammatical and conveys the same central condition less precisely.
questions.reasoning: The intended two-word phrase is exact, yet the head noun alone remains a true literal completion, so exact one-best scoring is unsafe.

questions.completedSentence: Planners compare shade with daily movements to find places where a small intervention could help many people.
evidenceQuotes: a small intervention would help many people
questions.competitorFailure: A map may inform planning, but the comparison identifies a place for an intervention, not a place where a map itself produces the benefit.
questions.reasoning: The summary closely paraphrases one source clause, including the adjective 'small' and the beneficiary phrase.

questions.completedSentence: In narrow streets, temporary canopies may cool people faster than trees.
evidenceQuotes: In narrow streets, temporary canopies, reflective surfaces or redesigned waiting areas may work faster
questions.competitorFailure: It creates the grammatically plausible phrase 'temporary reflective surfaces' and is another listed intervention covered by 'may work faster'; the text supplies no firm exclusion.
questions.reasoning: Canopies reproduce the exact local phrase, but the coordinated list makes reflective surfaces a second defensible passage span for the summary's broader cooling claim.

questions.completedSentence: Useful projects connect data collection with cooling plans that identify action, funding and feedback.
evidenceQuotes: connect data collection with cooling plans
questions.competitorFailure: It omits the purpose modifier, but 'plans that identify action, funding and feedback' remains grammatical and passage-supported.
questions.reasoning: The full phrase is more specific, yet the literal head noun alone also satisfies the frame and extraction rule.
